title: How to Apologize in Spanish: Perdón, Disculpe, Lo Siento
seo_title: How to Apologize in Spanish: Perdón, Disculpe, Lo Siento
meta_description: How to apologize in Spanish: perdón vs disculpe vs lo siento, apologies at work, for being late, formal apologies by email, and how to accept an apology.
excerpt: Perdón, disculpa or lo siento? Choosing the right apology for every situation.

body_html:
Knowing how to apologize in Spanish means choosing between several words that English translates as “sorry”. Perdón and disculpa work for small things, like bumping into someone. Lo siento expresses real regret or sympathy. Con permiso asks to get past. Use the wrong one and you may sound overly dramatic, or not sorry enough. Here’s how to pick the right apology in daily life, at work and in writing.

Key takeaways
  • Perdón / Perdona / Perdone: small mistakes and getting attention.
  • Disculpa / Disculpe: polite apologies and interruptions.
  • Lo siento: real regret, bad news and condolences.
  • Formal written apologies: Le pido disculpas por…
{{toc}}

How to apologize in Spanish: which word?

PhraseUse it forExample
PerdónSmall accidents, interrupting¡Perdón! Te he pisado. Sorry! I stepped on you.
Perdona / PerdoneGetting attention, small apologiesPerdone, ¿tiene hora? Excuse me, do you have the time?
Disculpa / DisculpePolite apologies, interruptionsDisculpa el retraso. Sorry for the delay.
Lo sientoReal regret, sympathyLo siento, no puedo ir. I’m sorry, I can’t go.
Con permisoPassing, leavingCon permiso, ¿puedo pasar?

The RAE dictionary defines disculpar as giving reasons to excuse a fault, and also as forgiving one, which is why disculpe works both to apologize and to excuse yourself.

Small, everyday apologies

  • ¡Uy, perdón! Oops, sorry!
  • Perdona, no te había visto. Sorry, I didn’t see you.
  • Disculpa, me he equivocado. Sorry, I made a mistake.
  • Perdona que te interrumpa. Sorry to interrupt you.
  • Perdona la molestia. Sorry to bother you.

Notice perdona que + subjunctive: Perdona que llegue tarde (Sorry I’m late).

Being late and canceling

  • Siento llegar tarde. I’m sorry I’m late.
  • Perdona el retraso, había mucho tráfico. Sorry for the delay, there was a lot of traffic.
  • Lo siento, al final no puedo ir. I’m sorry, I can’t make it after all.
  • Siento avisarte tan tarde. Sorry for letting you know so late.
{{image:2}}

Real regret: lo siento

Use lo siento when you feel genuinely bad, or to show sympathy:

  • Lo siento mucho, fue culpa mía. I’m really sorry, it was my fault.
  • Siento mucho lo que pasó. I’m very sorry about what happened.
  • Lo siento, no era mi intención. I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to.
  • Lo siento mucho por tu pérdida. I’m so sorry for your loss. (see {{link:condolences-in-spanish|condolences in Spanish}})

For apologies in a relationship, see {{link:apologizing-to-your-partner-in-spanish|apologizing to your partner in Spanish}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Apologizing at work and by email

Professional apologies are clear, brief and solution-focused. Common phrases include Disculpe las molestias (Sorry for the inconvenience), Le pido disculpas por el error (I apologize for the error), Lamentamos el retraso en la entrega (We regret the delay in delivery) and Ya lo hemos solucionado (We have already fixed it). Lamentar is the formal verb for “to regret”, typical in company emails and official notices. A good structure is: apologize, explain briefly, say what you’ve done, thank them for their patience: Gracias por su paciencia y comprensión. More in {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.

Accepting an apology

  • No pasa nada. It’s fine / No problem.
  • Tranquilo/a. Don’t worry.
  • No te preocupes. Don’t worry about it.
  • Disculpas aceptadas. Apology accepted.
  • Está todo bien. It’s all good.

A sample conversation

  • A: ¡Perdona que llegue tarde! El metro se ha parado. (Sorry I’m late! The metro stopped.)
  • B: Tranquila, no pasa nada. Acabo de llegar. (Don’t worry, it’s fine. I just got here.)
  • A: Aun así, lo siento. Te invito al café. (Even so, I’m sorry. The coffee’s on me.)

Cultural notes

In English we say “sorry” constantly: when someone bumps into us, when we ask a question, even when we’re not sure what we did. In Spanish, that much apologizing can sound odd or overly formal. When someone bumps into you, a quick perdón from either side is enough. When you need to pass someone, con permiso or perdón works better than lo siento. In Mexico and Colombia, qué pena or qué pena con usted is a common, gentle way to say “I’m sorry to bother you” or “how embarrassing”. See {{link:spanish-politeness-mistakes|Spanish politeness mistakes}}.

Apologies with explanations

Spanish speakers often soften an apology with es que… (it’s just that…), a very common way to give a reason: Perdona, es que no he visto tu mensaje hasta ahora (Sorry, it’s just that I didn’t see your message until now). It sounds natural and friendly, as long as the explanation doesn’t turn into an excuse. Other useful softeners are sin querer (by accident): Lo borré sin querer (I deleted it by accident), and no me di cuenta (I didn’t realize): Perdona, no me di cuenta de que estabas ocupado.

Apologizing to a group

When you speak to several people, change the verb: Perdonen or Disculpen, which work for any group in Latin America: Disculpen la espera (Sorry for the wait), Perdón a todos, ya llegué (Sorry, everyone, I’m here now). In Spain, friends use the vosotros form: Perdonad.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetterWhy
Lo siento to pass someonePerdón / Con permisoLo siento is too heavy
Perdón por tu pérdida.Lo siento mucho.Condolences need lo siento
Perdona que llego tarde.Perdona que llegue tarde.Subjunctive after perdona que
Estoy desolado for small thingsPerdonaOverly dramatic

Final thoughts

Small things: perdón or disculpa. Real regret: lo siento. Getting past: con permiso. Formal writing: le pido disculpas. Match the word to the moment and your apologies will sound natural. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between perdón, disculpa and lo siento?
faq.a: Perdón and disculpa are for small mistakes and getting attention. Lo siento expresses real regret or sympathy.

faq.q: How do you say “sorry I’m late” in Spanish?
faq.a: Siento llegar tarde, Perdona el retraso, or Perdona que llegue tarde.

faq.q: How do you apologize formally in Spanish?
faq.a: Le pido disculpas por…, Disculpe las molestias, or Lamentamos el retraso.
